**Prerequisites**
To run all the code in this manuscript, you will need the following software:
- FreeSurfer
- SimNIBS
- python
- git
- yq
We recommend you build a virtual environment for the python framework using conda. It is important that you use python version 3.11, the newest python version that lets all the used dependencies coexist. The virtual environment should then contain the mindmap package, specifically designed to hold any functions related to this project.
```bash
cd ~/location/for/mindmap/package
git clone https://github.com/NinoHerve/mindmap.git

cd ~/location/for/manuscript/project
git clone https://github.com/NinoHerve/wCSET.git

conda create -n <env-name> python=3.11
conda activate <env-name>
pip install .
```
You should now be ready to run anything that comes ahead.

# Materials and Methods

## Source Reconstruction Pipeline

### Source Space — Additional Implementation Details

**Surface reconstruction and dipole placement.** The cortical surface was reconstructed using FreeSurfer (v7.4.1). Dipoles were placed via an oct6 icosahedral subdivision (after excluding medial-wall and non-cortical vertices) using MNE-Python (v1.9.0; @gramfort_meg_2013).

**Orientation-constraint rationale.** Dipole orientations were fixed normal to the cortical manifold — a constraint widely adopted in distributed source imaging because the dominant contributors to the EEG signal, pyramidal neurons, have net dipole moments oriented normal to the cortical surface [@dale_improved_1993]. For the connectivity-informed methods, the constraint is also a structural requirement. The connectome describes connections between pairs of fixed cortical locations. Each location carries a single scalar source amplitude. A free-orientation dipole instead has three orthogonal components, which have no counterpart in the connectome.

### Volume Conduction Model — Additional Implementation Details

**Head-model pipeline.** Brain tissues were segmented into three compartments (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) using the SimNIBS CHARM pipeline (v4.5; @puonti_accurate_2020). Each compartment mask was smoothed via morphological closing and fitted with a deformable grade-5 icosahedral template, each surface constrained in turn to stay outside its inner neighbor's already-fitted surface (skin fitted last, constrained by the outer skull; outer skull constrained by the inner skull) — the "sequential and non-intersecting" fitting referenced in the main text.

**Skull-base limitation.** The boundary element method requires each tissue compartment to be a closed, watertight surface, but the true skull base is not: openings such as the foramen magnum and the smaller foramina nerves and vessels pass through break that assumption. Rather than attempt to model this genuinely perforated geometry, our fitting procedure simply closes the skull surfaces off smoothly below a fixed height, sacrificing anatomical accuracy at the very base of the skull by design. This is only acceptable if the resulting error stays away from the sources actually reconstructed here: @lanfer_skull_2012 found that errors from simplifying the inferior skull, while not negligible in general, concentrate in deep sources near the skull base (e.g., cerebellum) — a region this manuscript's cortical-surface-only source space never reconstructs from in the first place.

**Why the default watershed extraction is sub-optimal.** MNE-Python's default pipeline (`mne.bem.make_watershed_bem`, delegating to FreeSurfer's `mri_watershed`) fits the outer scalp surface directly from the T1 via a deformable surface fit, but T1-weighted MRI has poor bone contrast, so the inner and outer skull surfaces are not obtained the same principled way: the inner skull is instead approximated by expanding the brain mask outward by a fixed margin, and the outer skull by retracting the already-fit scalp surface inward, rather than by detecting the actual bone boundary. Neither is a genuine tissue-boundary detection step, which is why watershed-derived skull surfaces are a well-known source of geometry problems and MNE's own documentation recommends visually inspecting them before use — precisely the failure mode motivating this manuscript's custom CHARM-based pipeline instead.

**BEM comparison against MNE-Python's default watershed extraction.** To illustrate the sub-optimal geometries this produces, we additionally ran MNE-Python's default FreeSurfer watershed extraction (`mne.bem.make_watershed_bem`, FreeSurfer v7.4.1) on the flagship simulation subject (sub-10) and compared the resulting surfaces against the CHARM-based ones actually used for reconstruction (@tbl-bem-comparison). The default watershed geometry fails MNE's own BEM-construction check outright: calling `mne.make_bem_model` on it raises `RuntimeError: Surface inner skull is not completely inside surface outer skull`. Checking each compartment pair's nesting directly confirms why: 42/10,242 (0.41%) inner-skull vertices lie geometrically outside the outer-skull surface, and 4/10,242 (0.04%) outer-skull vertices lie outside the scalp, with the two skull surfaces coming within 0.32 mm of touching at their closest point. The CHARM-based pipeline's sequential, constrained fitting produces zero such violations by construction, with a comfortable 2.32 mm minimum gap between the skull surfaces, and its BEM model builds without error.

| Metric | MNE default watershed | Custom CHARM pipeline |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Inner-skull vertices outside outer-skull | 42 / 10,242 (0.41%) | 0 / 10,242 (0.00%) |
| Outer-skull vertices outside scalp | 4 / 10,242 (0.04%) | 0 / 10,242 (0.00%) |
| Minimum inner-to-outer-skull gap | 0.32 mm | 2.32 mm |
| Minimum outer-skull-to-scalp gap | 2.12 mm | 3.21 mm |
| `mne.make_bem_model` / `make_bem_solution` | Fails (nesting violation) | Succeeds |

: BEM geometry comparison for the flagship simulation subject (sub-10): MNE-Python's default watershed extraction vs. the custom CHARM-based pipeline used throughout this manuscript. {#tbl-bem-comparison}

**A second example where watershed does not fail outright.** The sub-10 case above is a hard failure — MNE refuses to build a BEM model at all. That is not the only failure mode: for subject sub-pat10 of the SPIKE resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A), the default watershed geometry *passes* MNE's nesting check (`mne.make_bem_model` and `mne.make_bem_solution` both succeed without error) and is still visibly wrong (@fig-bem-spike). Panel (a) shows CHARM's own tissue segmentation (`Bone-Cortical`/`Bone-Cancellous` in tan, `Skin` not shown) as anatomical reference for where the skull actually is — not independent ground truth, since panel (b)'s CHARM surface is fit directly from this same segmentation, but a meaningful check on panel (c)'s watershed surface, which never sees this segmentation at all. CHARM's outer-skull contour (panel b) closely follows the segmented bone boundary. Watershed's (panel c) does not: it balloons outward well past the true skull, consistent with the coarse expand-the-brain/retract-the-scalp heuristic described above rather than genuine bone detection.


**Skull-conductivity mismatch precedent.** A similar strategy — perturbing skull conductivity between the forward and inverse models to avoid the inverse crime — has been used elsewhere to probe the sensitivity of EEG source analysis to head-model mismatch [@vorwerk_skull_2014].

```{python filename="forward_mismatch_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import sys
import numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, "..")
from scripts.data_manager import SimfManager

# Self-contained, like the other Annex sections above: reloads the two
# forward solutions actually used for Study I (Section 2.1.2) rather than
# hand-computing this offline - processing_simf.qmd does not itself compute
# this comparison, so there is no cached result to reuse here.
dm_fwd = SimfManager("../processing/simf.config.yml")
sub_fwd = "10"
fwd_sim = dm_fwd.load(sub_fwd, "fwd", desc="sim")
fwd_inv = dm_fwd.load(sub_fwd, "fwd", desc="inv")

G_sim = fwd_sim["sol"]["data"]
G_inv = fwd_inv["sol"]["data"]

# Relative difference measure (RDM): per-dipole leadfield columns normalized
# to unit norm (removing amplitude scaling), then the norm of their
# difference - a standard forward-model comparison metric quantifying
# topographic (shape) mismatch, of the kind used in the head-model-mismatch
# literature (@vorwerk_skull_2014). 0 = identical topography, 2 = inverted.
G_sim_n = G_sim / np.linalg.norm(G_sim, axis=0, keepdims=True)
G_inv_n = G_inv / np.linalg.norm(G_inv, axis=0, keepdims=True)
rdm = np.linalg.norm(G_sim_n - G_inv_n, axis=0)

fwd_n_dipoles = f"{G_sim.shape[1]:,}"
fwd_rdm_median = fmt_num(np.median(rdm) * 100, 1)
fwd_rdm_mean = fmt_num(np.mean(rdm) * 100, 1)
fwd_rdm_iqr_lo = fmt_num(np.percentile(rdm, 25) * 100, 1)
fwd_rdm_iqr_hi = fmt_num(np.percentile(rdm, 75) * 100, 1)
```

**Forward-model mismatch magnitude.** Comparing the two forward solutions' gain matrices directly for the flagship simulation subject (sub-10, `{python} fwd_n_dipoles`-dipole source space): the relative difference measure (RDM) — a standard forward-model comparison metric quantifying topographic (shape) differences independently of amplitude scaling, the relevant summary of forward-model *mismatch* since a source-reconstruction method invariant to overall amplitude scaling would not be biased by gain differences alone — has a median of `{python} fwd_rdm_median`% across dipoles (mean `{python} fwd_rdm_mean`%, IQR [`{python} fwd_rdm_iqr_lo`%, `{python} fwd_rdm_iqr_hi`%]), consistent with the "~10%" figure quoted in the main text.

### Connectivity Matrices — Additional Implementation Details

This section provides implementation-level detail for the connectivity matrices described in Section 2.1.3.

**Empirical connectomes.** Short-range links connect each dipole to its geodesically nearest neighbors on the cortical manifold, subject to two constraints: a maximum geodesic distance of 15 mm, and a maximum of 8 such neighbors per dipole. The 15 mm threshold is reasonably well-grounded: at this source space's resolution it excludes only ~1% of true (Euclidean) nearest-neighbor pairs from being connected — down from ~6.4% at an earlier, coarser source-space resolution — and it also falls within the ~5–30 mm range typically cited for U-fiber length scales. The 8-neighbor cap is a softer, less rigorously-grounded choice: raised from an earlier value of 3 simply to preserve similar relative local coverage after dipole density roughly tripled at the current resolution (candidate neighbors within 15 mm rose from ~35 to ~88 per dipole), rather than derived from an independent criterion of its own.

**Atlas surrogate.** The MultiConn atlas reference population used to define long-range tracts comprises 66 subjects, and a tract is retained only if present across all 66. Rather than connecting every dipole pair between two atlas-connected regions, only a fraction of the possible dipole-to-dipole edges is instantiated, at a sparsity level (14%) determined by matching the edge density of this same sub-10 subject's own empirical connectome (above) — the only subject in our sample with real tractography data available.

**Local surrogate.** Nodes are additionally connected across hemispheres to their homotopic (mirror-symmetric) partner to keep the resulting graph connected.

**Beltrami-operator surrogate.** Eigenmodes are computed using the `lapy` Python library (v1.6.0) for the underlying finite-element stiffness/mass matrix assembly. This mesh is the triangulation of the source space itself, in dipole space (Section 2.1.1) — the decimated, cortex-only surface used for the dipoles — rather than the dense FreeSurfer surface typically used for this computation. This matches @wang_geometry_2026's own approach: their Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes are likewise computed on their own downsampled, dipole-resolution source space (~10,000 dipoles per hemisphere for real data, ~4,000 per hemisphere for their benchmark simulations — comparable in spirit to this manuscript's own ~7,600-dipole source space) rather than the dense native FreeSurfer mesh; their Discussion's contrast against "coarse regional parcellations" refers to connectome/atlas-eigenmode approaches like CSET, not to mesh density.

**Harmonic localization (inverse participation ratio).** The Discussion hypothesizes that the true connectome underperforms its dMRI-free surrogates in Study I because its reconstruction-weighted harmonics are more spatially localized. @fig-ipr-harmonics quantifies this: for each condition, every harmonic's inverse participation ratio (IPR) — $\sum_i x_i^4$ for an orthonormal harmonic $x$, higher for harmonics concentrated on fewer dipoles — is weighted by wCSET's own reconstruction weight for that harmonic (Section 2.1.4) and averaged, excluding each condition's trivial constant mode(s) (maximally spread by construction, regardless of graph structure). The true connectome's weighted-mean IPR is higher than every graph-based surrogate's and higher than beltrami's — consistent with a more rigid, spatially specific prior that helps only when it matches genuine tract-driven clustering.

```{python filename="simf_ipr_harmonics_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-ipr-harmonics
#| fig-cap: "Reconstruction-weighted mean inverse participation ratio (IPR) of each condition's harmonics (subject sub-10) — the basis wCSET's spatial prior is built from. Higher IPR means harmonics concentrated on fewer, sometimes spatially disjoint dipoles; lower IPR means harmonics that vary smoothly across the cortex. The true connectome (original) produces more localized harmonics than every dMRI-free surrogate."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "..")
from scripts.data_manager import SimfManager

# Reproduces surrogate_harmonics_investigation.ipynb's weighted-mean-IPR
# result under the reader-facing surrogate names used throughout this
# manuscript (Section 2.1.3) rather than the on-disk `Surrogate` tags.
dm_ipr = SimfManager("../processing/simf.config.yml")
sub_ipr = "10"

LOWPASS_CONDS = ["original", "fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin"]
HARM = 5
LOGPASS_CUTOFF = 150
ALL_CONDS = LOWPASS_CONDS + ["beltrami"]

IPR_LABELS = {
    "original": "original", "beltrami": "beltrami",
    "fused": "atlas", "fused-bin": "atlas-bin",
    "geom-atlas": "local", "geom-atlas-bin": "local-bin",
}
IPR_COLORS = {
    "original": LINE_COLOR, "beltrami": "#2a78d6",
    "fused": "#eb6834", "fused-bin": "#1baf7a",
    "geom-atlas": "#eda100", "geom-atlas-bin": "#e87ba4",
}

def _load_eig(desc):
    kwargs = {} if desc == "original" else {"desc": desc}
    eig = dm_ipr.load(sub_ipr, "eig", **kwargs)
    return eig["vec"], eig["val"]

eigs_ipr = {d: _load_eig(d) for d in ALL_CONDS}

# wCSET's own reconstruction weight per harmonic (Section 2.1.4): exponential
# lowpass (harm=5) for the true connectome and its four graph-based
# surrogates, GBF's logpass/cutoff=150 for beltrami - the same two
# weighting mechanisms used throughout the manuscript, not recomputed
# differently here.
def _lowpass_weight(val, harm=HARM):
    return np.exp(-harm * val)

def _logpass_weight(val, cutoff=LOGPASS_CUTOFF):
    w = np.zeros_like(val)
    lam_cutoff = val[cutoff - 1]
    normalized = np.clip(val[:cutoff] / lam_cutoff, 1e-8, 1.0)
    w[:cutoff] = np.sqrt(-np.log(normalized))
    return w

weights_ipr = {name: _lowpass_weight(eigs_ipr[name][1]) for name in LOWPASS_CONDS}
weights_ipr["beltrami"] = _logpass_weight(eigs_ipr["beltrami"][1])

# Inverse participation ratio: IPR = sum(x_i^4) for an orthonormal harmonic x
# (sum(x_i^2)=1) - a condensed-matter-physics measure of how localized a
# wavefunction (here, a cortical harmonic) is.
def _ipr(eigvec):
    p = eigvec ** 2
    return np.sum(p ** 2, axis=0)

iprs_ipr = {name: _ipr(eigs_ipr[name][0]) for name in ALL_CONDS}

# Reconstruction-weighted mean IPR, one number per condition - excludes each
# condition's trivial constant/near-constant mode(s) (k=0 for the graph
# Laplacian conditions; k=0,1 for beltrami, one per independently-solved
# hemisphere), which carry the top weight by construction but are, by
# definition, maximally spread out regardless of graph structure.
ipr_summary = {}
for name in LOWPASS_CONDS:
    w, p = weights_ipr[name][1:], iprs_ipr[name][1:]
    ipr_summary[name] = np.sum(w * p) / np.sum(w)
w_b, p_b = weights_ipr["beltrami"][2:], iprs_ipr["beltrami"][2:]
ipr_summary["beltrami"] = np.sum(w_b * p_b) / np.sum(w_b)

ipr_order = ["original", "fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin", "beltrami"]

ipr_fig, ipr_ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5))
ipr_ax.bar(
    range(len(ipr_order)), [ipr_summary[n] for n in ipr_order],
    color=[IPR_COLORS[n] for n in ipr_order],
)
ipr_ax.set_ylabel("Reconstruction-weighted mean IPR")
ipr_ax.set_xticks(range(len(ipr_order)))
ipr_ax.set_xticklabels([IPR_LABELS[n] for n in ipr_order], rotation=30, ha="right")
ipr_ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
```

To make "IPR" concrete rather than abstract, @fig-ipr-example renders two actual harmonics from the true connectome's own spectrum, both drawn from the same low-frequency band (k=1–30) that carries the largest individual per-harmonic weight in wCSET's reconstruction (Section 2.1.4) — so the visual difference between them reflects localization, not frequency. The lowest-IPR harmonic in that band (k=`{python} k_lo_ipr`, IPR=`{python} ipr_lo_val`) is spread smoothly across almost the entire cortex, essentially a single left-right gradient; the highest-IPR harmonic (k=`{python} k_hi_ipr`, IPR=`{python} ipr_hi_val`, ~`{python} ipr_ratio_val`× higher) instead concentrates its activity onto a few disjoint patches. This is what "more spatially concentrated" means for the true connectome's weighted-mean IPR above: not that every harmonic it relies on looks like the right-hand panel, but that its harmonics tend further in that direction than the surrogates'.

```{python filename="simf_ipr_example_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-ipr-example
#| fig-cap: "Example low-frequency harmonics (k=1-30 band) of the true connectome (subject sub-10), illustrating what inverse participation ratio (IPR) means spatially. Left: the lowest-IPR harmonic in this band, spread smoothly across the cortex. Right: the highest-IPR harmonic in this band, concentrated onto a few disjoint patches. Dorsal view, both hemispheres."
import mindmap as mm
import pyvista as pv
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

pv.OFF_SCREEN = True

# Restrict the example search to the same low-frequency band (k=1-30,
# excluding the trivial k=0 constant mode) that dominates wCSET's
# per-harmonic weight, rather than searching the full spectrum - a harmonic
# with extreme IPR far out in the spectrum wouldn't illustrate what the
# weighted-mean IPR above is actually summarizing.
ipr_band = range(1, 31)
iprs_original = iprs_ipr["original"]
k_lo_ipr = min(ipr_band, key=lambda k: iprs_original[k])
k_hi_ipr = max(ipr_band, key=lambda k: iprs_original[k])

ipr_lo_val = fmt_stat(iprs_original[k_lo_ipr], 4)
ipr_hi_val = fmt_stat(iprs_original[k_hi_ipr], 4)
ipr_ratio_val = fmt_num(iprs_original[k_hi_ipr] / iprs_original[k_lo_ipr], 1)

# Reloads the forward solution just for its source space (dipole positions/
# hemisphere split) - not otherwise needed by this section, so not part of
# the shared eigs_ipr/dm_ipr setup above.
src_ipr = dm_ipr.load(sub_ipr, "fwd", desc="sim")["src"]
vec_original = eigs_ipr["original"][0]

ipr_example_panel = (
    mm.viz.BrainPlot.from_source_space(
        src_ipr, values=vec_original[:, k_lo_ipr], states=[0],
        title=f"k={k_lo_ipr} (low IPR)", view="dorsal",
    )
    | mm.viz.BrainPlot.from_source_space(
        src_ipr, values=vec_original[:, k_hi_ipr], states=[0],
        title=f"k={k_hi_ipr} (high IPR)", view="dorsal",
    )
)
ipr_example_img = ipr_example_panel.screenshot()

ipr_example_fig, ipr_example_ax = plt.subplots(
    figsize=(ipr_example_img.shape[1] / 130, ipr_example_img.shape[0] / 130)
)
ipr_example_ax.imshow(ipr_example_img)
ipr_example_ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
```

### Inverse Problem and Methods — Additional Details

**Standard inverse solutions — full derivation.** This section provides the full derivation of the standard inverse solutions (wMNE, dSPM, sLORETA) introduced in Section 2.1.4.

From a Bayesian perspective, $\mathbf s$ is treated as a random variable with a prior distribution $P(\mathbf s)$ [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Assuming a Gaussian prior $\mathbf s \sim \mathcal N(0, \Sigma_{\mathbf s})$, reconstruction becomes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation, leading to the optimization problem given in Eq. (1) of the main text. There, $\mathbf C$ acts as a weighting matrix derived from the prior covariance, such that $\mathbf C^T\mathbf C = \mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s}^{-1}$. In practice, the true source covariance $\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$ is unknown and replaced with the identity matrix — the assumption of independent, equal-variance sources that gives wMNE, dSPM and sLORETA their "independent-source" label throughout this work.

wMNE additionally adjusts source variances, generating the depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d$ applied to counteract the bias of $l_2$-regularized solutions toward superficial dipoles:

$$
\mathbf \Sigma_{\mathbf s} = \mathbf W_d^2, \qquad \text{where} \quad W_{d,ii} = \lVert \mathbf L_{:i}\rVert^{-\kappa}
$$

so that deep sources, with small lead-field norms, receive a larger prior variance. In the SVD form of the main text, $\mathbf B=\mathbf W_d$.

For wMNE, the depth-weighting exponent was set to $\kappa=0.8$, the MEG-optimized value reported by @lin_assessing_2006 (who found a higher optimal range, 2.0–5.0, for EEG specifically). sLORETA and dSPM apply an additional post-hoc standardization on top of the minimum-norm estimate, and were run without additional depth weighting, since this noise-normalization step already compensates for depth bias on its own.

With $\mathbf B=\mathbf I$ and the SVD $\mathbf L=\mathbf E_f\boldsymbol\Gamma\mathbf E_\ell^\top$ of the main text, both standardizations divide the minimum-norm estimate $s^*_k$ of source $k$ by a norm computed from the same decomposition:

$$
z_k^{\text{dSPM}}=\frac{s^*_k}{\lVert[\mathbf E_\ell\mathbf D_\lambda]_{k,:}\rVert},\qquad
z_k^{\text{sLORETA}}=\frac{s^*_k}{\big\lVert[\mathbf E_\ell\,\mathrm{diag}(\gamma_j/\sqrt{\gamma_j^2+\lambda})]_{k,:}\big\rVert}
$$

The dSPM denominator is the noise standard deviation of source $k$, since the whitened noise has identity covariance [@dale_dynamic_2000]. The sLORETA denominator is the square root of the $k$-th diagonal entry of the resolution matrix [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002]. MNE-Python's sLORETA factor differs from this one by the constant $1/\sqrt\lambda$, which rescales the maps without changing their shape [@gramfort_meg_2013].

**GBF — full formulation.** wCSET (Eq. 4) is reconfigured to approximate GBF via three changes to its own formulation: (i) $\mathbf U$ becomes the Laplace-Beltrami eigenbasis of the cortical mesh (Section 2.1.3) rather than the connectome's; (ii) no depth weighting ($\mathbf W_d = \mathbf I$); and (iii) the exponential weights (Eq. 3) become GBF's hard-truncated, log-form weighting, $W_{h,ii} = \sqrt{-\log(\mu_i/\mu_S)}$ for the $S$ lowest-frequency Beltrami eigenmodes and $W_{h,ii}=0$ beyond ($\mu_i$: Laplace-Beltrami eigenvalues).

**GBF cutoff tuning.** Wang et al. tune a scale parameter $\beta$ for their log-form weighting, but our pipeline trace-renormalizes the inverse kernel before the ridge solve (standard practice), which renders $\beta$ a pure rescale with no effect on the reconstruction. Rather than leave this comparator's one nominally free parameter untuned, we instead tuned the parameter that actually shapes the weighting under our normalization, the cutoff $S$: a sweep against simulated ground truth showed $S=150$ roughly halving peak-localization error relative to $S=300$ (6.1 vs. 14.7 mm) while matching or exceeding it on average precision.

## Datasets and Study-Specific Settings

### Synthetic Data — Data Acquisition and Preprocessing

This section lists the data needed to reproduce the synthetic data described in Section 2.2.1, and the processing applied to it before simulation. The corresponding code is in `processing_simf.qmd` of the manuscript repository ([github.com/NinoHerve/wCSET](https://github.com/NinoHerve/wCSET)).

**Data source.** All subject data come from the VEPCON dataset [@pascucci_source_2022], publicly available on OpenNeuro as dataset ds003505 ([openneuro.org/datasets/ds003505](https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds003505); paths below as of snapshot 1.1.2). Only one participant, `sub-10`, is used. None of VEPCON's EEG recordings, raw diffusion images or other participants are needed.

| File (relative to the dataset root) | Content | Used for |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `sub-10/anat/sub-10_T1w.nii.gz` | Raw T1-weighted MRI | CHARM tissue segmentation (BEM) |
| `derivatives/freesurfer-7.1.1/sub-10/` | FreeSurfer reconstruction (whole subject folder) | Source space, parcellation, electrode coregistration |
| `derivatives/cmp-v3.0.3/sub-10/dwi/sub-10_model-CSD_desc-DET_tractogram.trk` | Whole-brain tractogram, in diffusion space | Long-range connectome edges |
| `derivatives/cmp-v3.0.3/sub-10/xfm/final0GenericAffine.mat` | Affine registration between T1w and diffusion space (ANTs) | Mapping streamline endpoints to T1w space |

: VEPCON files required for the synthetic data. {#tbl-vepcon-files}

**Tractogram provenance.** The tractogram is used as distributed, without re-running tractography. According to its Connectome Mapper 3 configuration file (`derivatives/cmp-v3.0.3/sub-10/sub-10_diffusion_config.json`), the diffusion data were corrected for eddy currents and motion (FSL `eddy_correct`), without denoising or bias-field correction. Fiber orientations were reconstructed with constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD, maximal harmonic order 4) in MRtrix3. One million streamlines were then generated with deterministic tractography (`SD_stream`; step 0.5 mm, length 5–200 mm, maximum angle 45°, FOD cutoff 0.05), without anatomically-constrained tractography (ACT), and filtered with SIFT. These settings come from a later Connectome Mapper release than the one described in @pascucci_source_2022, and differ from the tractograms that @ruequeralt_connectome_2024 recomputed from the same raw DWI for CSET (10 million streamlines with ACT, after denoising and bias-field correction).

**External resources.** Besides VEPCON, the pipeline uses:

- the EGI 256-channel HydroCel template montage built into MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013], used as sensor layout (no subject-specific electrode positions);
- the Lausanne 2018 scale-4 cortical atlas and the HCP probabilistic thalamic-nuclei atlas, with the MNI ICBM152 2009c template, needed to build the MultiConn parcellation [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022];
- the MultiConn probabilistic connectivity atlas at scale 4 [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], needed only for the atlas surrogate (Section 2.1.3).

**Processing steps.** Everything else is derived from the files above:

1. *Head model.* The T1w is segmented with SimNIBS CHARM [@puonti_accurate_2020], and the three BEM surfaces (inner skull, outer skull, scalp) are built from this segmentation (Volume Conduction Model, below).
2. *Parcellation.* The MultiConn scale-4 parcellation is computed on the FreeSurfer reconstruction (white-matter margin 2 mm; thalamic atlas thresholded at probability 0.05). Its cortical labels provide the cortex mask and the 446 regions used for the probe set.
3. *Source space.* Dipoles are placed on the FreeSurfer white-matter surface (oct6 spacing) and restricted to the cortex mask (Source Space, below).
4. *Electrodes.* The EGI template is reduced by removing the same cheek electrodes as in Clinical Dataset A (Section 2.2.2). It is aligned to the subject with a rigid fiducial-based registration, and each electrode is then projected radially onto the CHARM scalp surface.
5. *Connectome.* Streamline endpoints are mapped from diffusion space to T1w space with the affine transform above (the nonlinear `final1Warp.nii.gz` is not used). Streamlines are kept only if both endpoints fall in the cortex mask. Each remaining endpoint is assigned to a dipole within 4 mm, and each edge is weighted by fiber length. Short-range gray-matter edges are then added where tractography found none (Connectivity Matrices, below).

### Synthetic Data — Additional Simulation Details

This section provides implementation-level detail for the synthetic data described in Section 2.2.1.

| Parameter | Symbol | Value | Unit | Description | Ref. |
|:---|:---:|---:|:---:|:---|:---:|
| Spike duration | $W$ | 0.05 | s | Total duration of the double-Hanning-window spike waveform. | [@kane_revised_2017] |
| Axonal conduction speed (long-range) | $v(l>35)$ | 4.5 | mm/ms | Conduction speed for long-range (non-U-fiber) tracts, i.e. edges longer than the U-fiber length cutoff. | [@lemarechal_brain_2022; @van_blooijs_developmental_2023] |
| U-fiber conduction speed | $v(l\leq35)$ | 2.5 | mm/ms | Conduction speed for short-range U-fibers (edges at or below the U-fiber length cutoff), distinctly slower than long-range tracts. | [@van_blooijs_developmental_2023] |
| U-fiber maximum length | — | 35 | mm | Length cutoff separating U-fibers from long-range tracts. | — |
| Nodal delay per hop | $\tau_p$ | 7 | ms | Per-hop relay delay representing the time a cortical population takes to receive, integrate, and re-fire an input; accumulated once per edge on the propagation path. | [@lemarechal_brain_2022] |
| Spatial decay factor | $\gamma$ | 0.5 | — | Per-hop amplitude decay factor applied to propagating activity; a tuned/free parameter, since no literature value exists for this quantity. | — |
| Delay jitter (s.d., per hop) | $\sigma_\tau$ | 1 | ms | Per-hop timing-jitter standard deviation, accumulated as jitter$\times\sqrt{\text{hops}}$ along the propagation path to avoid deterministic, sample-locked arrival times. | — |
| Sensor noise floor (fixed) | — | 2.0 | µV RMS | Fixed instrument/electrode-noise floor added at the sensor level, independent of the source-space noise contribution. | — |
| Target sensor noise (total) | — | 15.0 | µV RMS | Target total delivered sensor-level background noise (instrument floor plus forward-projected source-space noise). | [@nunez_electric_2006] |
| Target SNR | — | 5 | — | Target single-trial peak-amplitude SNR used to scale source activity before sensor projection. | [@gonsisko_electroencephalographic_2024] |
| Source regions (probe set) | — | 100 | — | Number of source regions simulated, drawn from the shared spatially-uniform (farthest-point-sampled) probe set. | — |
| Repetitions per region | — | 8 | — | Number of repeated simulations per source region (independent noise draws), set via power analysis. | — |

: Simulation parameters. Dashes mark free/tuned parameters with no literature-derived value. {#tbl-sim-params}

**Propagation model rationale.** A neural mass model [@jansen_electroencephalogram_1995] would capture propagation more physiologically, but such models become unstable at high mass counts, since network size and coupling strength jointly determine dynamical stability [@sanz-leon_mathematical_2015] — which is why other source-reconstruction studies typically cap the number of masses around 1,000, with dipoles spaced roughly 1 cm apart [@siu_structural_2026], a spacing at which the forward model's own point-dipole assumption starts to break down [@nunez_multi-scale_2019]. Our patch-seeded, connectome-driven propagation model avoids this trade-off, keeping the dipole model at high resolution (~7,600 dipoles, ~3.3 mm spacing) while remaining simple enough to generate realistic EEG spikes; we do not claim it is more faithful to reality than neural mass or field models, only that it offers insight a simple patch simulation cannot while staying tractable at high dipole counts.

**Spike waveform.** The spike waveform is a double Hanning window, following the same construction as @dewouters_source-reconstructed_2026:

$$
s_0(t) = \begin{cases} h\!\left(t,\, \tfrac{2}{3}W\right) & 0 \leq t \leq \tfrac{2}{3}W \\[4pt] -\tfrac{1}{2}\,h\!\left(t - \tfrac{2}{3}W,\; \tfrac{1}{3}W\right) & \tfrac{2}{3}W < t \leq W \end{cases}
$$

where $h(t, T) = \frac{1}{2}\!\left[1 - \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi t}{T}\right)\right]$ is a Hanning window of duration $T$, and $W = 0.05$ s (50 ms) is the total spike duration, chosen to fall centrally within the consensus clinical EEG duration convention for interictal spikes specifically (20–70 ms) [@kane_revised_2017].

**Propagation delay model.** The total propagation delay $\tau_j$ to dipole $j$ was computed as the sum of per-edge delays along the shortest path from the source:

$$
\tau_j = \sum_{(u,v)\,\in\,\mathcal{P}_j} \!\left(\frac{l_{uv}}{v(l_{uv})} + \tau_p\right) + \epsilon_\tau, \qquad v(l) = \begin{cases} 4.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l > 35 \text{ mm (long-range)} \\ 2.5 \text{ mm/ms} & l \leq 35 \text{ mm (U-fiber)} \end{cases}
$$

where $l_{uv}$ is the fiber length of edge $(u,v)$ in mm, and $v(l_{uv})$ is a conduction speed that depends on fiber length: 4.5 mm/ms for long-range tracts above 35 mm — the central estimate of two independent large-sample cortico-cortical evoked potential (CCEP) studies converging on ~3–6 m/s for adult long-range association fibers [@lemarechal_brain_2022; @van_blooijs_developmental_2023] — and a slower 2.5 mm/ms for short-range U-fibers at or below 35 mm, reflecting their distinctly slower reported conduction (~2–3 m/s) relative to long-range tracts [@van_blooijs_developmental_2023]. $\tau_p = 7$ ms is a fixed nodal delay per hop representing synaptic transmission plus relay latency, consistent with the population-level excitatory/inhibitory synaptic time constants (5.8–7.3 ms) estimated directly from CCEP modelling [@lemarechal_brain_2022]. $\epsilon_\tau \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\tau)$, with $\sigma_\tau = 1$ ms, is a per-dipole jitter term modelling uncertainty in propagation timing, accumulated once per hop along the shortest path (i.e. scaling with $\sqrt{h_j}$ rather than a single flat perturbation of the total path delay).

**Noise model derivation.** Sensor-level noise comprised a small fixed instrument/electrode-noise floor (2.0 µV RMS) plus a source-space contribution solved to bring the total delivered sensor-level baseline noise to a target of 15.0 µV RMS — the literature midpoint of the commonly-cited ~10–20 µV RMS scalp EEG background noise range [@nunez_electric_2006]. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was calibrated to a fixed single-trial target of 5 (peak amplitude relative to baseline standard deviation) by scaling the source activity prior to sensor projection: this sits above the ~2.0–3.2 linear-ratio range reported for single-trial interictal spikes [@gonsisko_electroencephalographic_2024], chosen as a practical compromise to keep delivered spikes comfortably above the simulator's own noise floor while remaining much closer to the single-trial literature range than a post-averaging-scale target would be.

**Power analysis.** The number of regions (100) and repetitions (8) per region were set via a power analysis targeting adequate power for the region-paired method comparisons reported throughout the Results, ensuring that the relative ranking of reconstruction methods is robust across a spatially-diverse sample of source regions rather than reflecting any single one; the main effect of method alone was already saturated at power ≈ 1.0 across every tested design.

### Clinical Dataset A — Additional Details

This section provides additional preprocessing detail for the resection cohort described in Section 2.2.2.

**Preprocessing by the data providers.** Data-provider preprocessing (per @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025) included bandpass filtering (high-pass: 0.3–1 Hz; low-pass: 30–100 Hz, with filter settings varying across patients due to the longitudinal nature of the dataset), downsampling to 250 Hz, and interpolation of noisy channels from neighbouring electrodes using 3D splines.

### Clinical Dataset B — Additional Details

This section provides additional recruitment, implantation, and ethics detail for the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort described in Section 2.2.3, drawn from @roehri_scalp-negative_2025, the source study for this cohort.

**Recruitment and implantation.** Patients were recruited at the EEG and Epilepsy Unit, Geneva University Hospital, among consecutive patients who underwent simultaneous iEEG–hdEEG recording between 2014 and 2019 during presurgical evaluation for pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy. Intracranial recordings used stereo-EEG (SEEG) intracerebral macroelectrodes implanted per standard clinical presurgical planning; the simultaneous recording session was performed on the last day before iEEG electrode removal, pairing the SEEG with a 257-channel geodesic scalp EEG net (Electrical Geodesic Inc.).

**Ethics approval.** The study was approved by the Geneva Regional Research Ethics Committee (protocol 13-004).

**MRI sequencing parameters.** The T1-weighted scan was acquired on a 3-T scanner (Siemens Prisma); @roehri_scalp-negative_2025 does not report further sequence parameters (TR/TE/voxel size).

**Comparison window.** The window over which virtual and recorded iEEG were compared was the continuous interval over which the evoked response's global field power (GFP) stayed above 3 standard deviations of the pre-spike baseline.

## Statistical Analysis — Additional Details

**Autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size.** For the paired t-test with effective sample size (used for Study 3's channel/timepoint comparisons), the effective sample size is computed as $n_{\text{eff}} = n / (1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{K} \rho_k)$, where $\rho_k$ is the paired-difference series' own lag-$k$ autocorrelation, summed until it falls within the white-noise 95% confidence band ($1.96/\sqrt{n}$), capped at $n/4$ — the standard correction for testing the mean of a serially-correlated series. This down-weights the nominal pair count to reflect the true amount of independent evidence when neighbouring channels or timepoints are correlated.

**Cluster-based permutation testing.** Continuous comparisons (e.g. across SNR or connectome perturbation severity) used a one-sample, sign-flip permutation test on the paired-difference series (MNE-Python's `permutation_cluster_1samp_test`; 3000 permutations), which identifies contiguous clusters of the coordinate where the two methods differ, rather than testing each point independently. The cluster-forming threshold matched the test's own two-tailed α = 0.05 default; each cluster's p-value reflects how extreme its summed test statistic is relative to the permutation null, and effect size (Cohen's dz) is computed from each subject's difference averaged across the cluster's span.

### Robustness to Data Noise — Full Results (Section 3.1.2)

```{python filename="simf_noise_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

noise_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("../results/simf/noise_sweep")
competitors = [m for m in METHODS if m != "wcset"]

# region-as-subject cluster-permutation summary vs. wCSET, every competitor
# on one shared axes - "compact version" pattern from
# mindmap/tutorials/analysis/metrics/metricsuite-noisesweep.ipynb. Region is
# the repeated-measures unit (the same physical region at every SNR level;
# repetitions aren't matched across levels, since each draws its own
# independent seed), SNR level is the swept coordinate, tested via
# mne.stats.permutation_cluster_1samp_test. noise_sweep_comparison.py
# registers `region`. Unlike the tutorial's correlation_pp example,
# localization_error_qrp is lower-is-better (mm to the true source), hence
# higher_is_better=False. Identical call to the one already cached by
# processing_simf.qmd's Statistics section.
noise_loc_snr_order = sorted(
    noise_metrics.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp"})["snr"].unique(), reverse=True
)

noise_loc_results = noise_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation(
    "localization_error", coord="snr", group_by="Method",
    comparisons=noise_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors), pairing_col="region",
    coord_order=noise_loc_snr_order, higher_is_better=False, filters={"phase": "qrp"},
    n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
)

# statistics quoted in the prose below. main_cluster() always returns the
# largest-mass cluster regardless of significance, so its result must be
# checked against "p_corrected" before being described as significant in
# prose: wMNE and dSPM each have one cluster that survives FDR correction;
# sLORETA's largest cluster does not. CSET is a further step down from
# that: its clusters_by_pair table against wCSET is entirely empty (no
# candidate cluster of either sign anywhere in the SNR range), so
# main_cluster() can't be called on it at all - handled separately below
# rather than assumed non-empty like the other three competitors.
noise_loc_wmne = main_cluster(noise_loc_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", "wmne")])
noise_loc_sloreta = main_cluster(noise_loc_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", "sloreta")])
noise_loc_cset_clusters = noise_loc_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", "cset")]
noise_loc_dspm = main_cluster(noise_loc_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", "dspm")])

noise_loc_wmne_p = fmt_p(noise_loc_wmne["p_corrected"])
noise_loc_wmne_dz = fmt_stat(noise_loc_wmne["effect_size"])
noise_loc_wmne_snr_start = fmt_num(noise_loc_wmne["snr_start"], 0)

noise_loc_sloreta_p = fmt_p(noise_loc_sloreta["p_corrected"])
noise_loc_sloreta_dz = fmt_stat(noise_loc_sloreta["effect_size"])
noise_loc_sloreta_snr = fmt_num(noise_loc_sloreta["snr_start"], 0)
noise_loc_sloreta_snr_end = fmt_num(noise_loc_sloreta["snr_end"], 0)

# No p_corrected/effect_size to quote when no cluster exists at all - the
# prose below states this directly instead of quoting cluster statistics.
noise_loc_cset_has_cluster = not noise_loc_cset_clusters.empty

noise_loc_dspm_p = fmt_p(noise_loc_dspm["p_corrected"])
noise_loc_dspm_dz = fmt_stat(noise_loc_dspm["effect_size"])
noise_loc_dspm_snr_start = fmt_num(noise_loc_dspm["snr_start"], 0)
noise_loc_dspm_snr_end = fmt_num(noise_loc_dspm["snr_end"], 0)

_loc_medians = noise_metrics.metadata["derived"]["loc_median"]
noise_loc_wmne_median20 = fmt_num(_loc_medians["wmne"][str(float(20))])
noise_loc_wmne_median1 = fmt_num(_loc_medians["wmne"][str(float(1))])
noise_loc_dspm_median1 = fmt_num(_loc_medians["dspm"][str(float(1))])
noise_loc_wcset_median1 = fmt_num(_loc_medians["wcset"][str(float(1))])

# Same region-as-subject cluster-permutation summary, once per phase -
# correlation is higher-is-better (unlike localization error), matching the
# tutorial's own correlation_pp example directly. Identical calls to the
# ones already cached by processing_simf.qmd's Statistics section.
noise_corr_snr_order = sorted(
    noise_metrics.to_df(metrics="correlation", filters={"phase": "qrp"})["snr"].unique(), reverse=True
)

noise_corr_results = {}
for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]:
    noise_corr_results[phase] = noise_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation(
        "correlation", coord="snr", group_by="Method",
        comparisons=noise_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors), pairing_col="region",
        coord_order=noise_corr_snr_order, higher_is_better=True, filters={"phase": phase},
        n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
    )

# statistics quoted in the prose below: largest-mass cluster per competitor
# per phase (all share p_corrected=0.001, so a single formatted value covers
# every one of them), plus the min/max effect size across all 8 (4
# competitors x 2 phases) to state the range quoted in prose, and wCSET's
# own median correlation at the SNR extremes.
# Only clusters where wCSET is better (sign = +1): below SNR 3 the clusters reverse (wCSET slightly
# lower while every correlation is near zero) and can have the larger mass.
def _better_cluster(phase, comp):
    clusters = noise_corr_results[phase].clusters_by_pair[("wcset", comp)]
    return main_cluster(clusters[clusters["sign"] == 1])

def _worse_cluster(phase, comp):
    clusters = noise_corr_results[phase].clusters_by_pair[("wcset", comp)]
    rows = clusters[clusters["sign"] == -1]
    return None if rows.empty else main_cluster(rows)

_all_dz = {}
for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]:
    for comp in competitors:
        _all_dz[(phase, comp)] = _better_cluster(phase, comp)["effect_size"]

noise_corr_p_all = fmt_p(max(_better_cluster(ph, c)["p_corrected"] for ph in ["qrp", "pp"] for c in competitors))
noise_corr_end_std = fmt_num(max(_better_cluster(ph, c)["snr_end"] for ph in ["qrp", "pp"] for c in ["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]), 0)
noise_corr_end_cset = fmt_num(max(_better_cluster(ph, "cset")["snr_end"] for ph in ["qrp", "pp"]), 0)
_worse = [w for w in (_worse_cluster(ph, c) for ph in ["qrp", "pp"] for c in competitors) if w is not None]
noise_corr_worse_p_max = f'{max(w["p_corrected"] for w in _worse):.3f}'
noise_corr_dz_min_key = min(_all_dz, key=lambda k: _all_dz[k])
noise_corr_dz_max_key = max(_all_dz, key=lambda k: _all_dz[k])
noise_corr_dz_min = fmt_stat(_all_dz[noise_corr_dz_min_key])
noise_corr_dz_max = fmt_stat(_all_dz[noise_corr_dz_max_key])
_phase_name = lambda p: "quarter rising phase" if p == "qrp" else "peak phase"
noise_corr_dz_min_label = f"{METHOD_LABELS[noise_corr_dz_min_key[1]]} at {_phase_name(noise_corr_dz_min_key[0])}"
noise_corr_dz_max_label = f"{METHOD_LABELS[noise_corr_dz_max_key[1]]} at {_phase_name(noise_corr_dz_max_key[0])}"

_corr_medians_qrp = noise_metrics.metadata["derived"]["corr_qrp_median"]
_corr_medians_pp = noise_metrics.metadata["derived"]["corr_pp_median"]
noise_corr_wcset_qrp20 = fmt_num(_corr_medians_qrp["wcset"][str(float(20))], 2)
noise_corr_wcset_qrp1 = fmt_num(_corr_medians_qrp["wcset"][str(float(1))], 2)
noise_corr_wcset_pp20 = fmt_num(_corr_medians_pp["wcset"][str(float(20))], 2)
noise_corr_wcset_pp1 = fmt_num(_corr_medians_pp["wcset"][str(float(1))], 2)
```

To assess whether the improvements shown above survive noisier measurement conditions, we swept the simulated target SNR from 20 down to 1 and repeated source reconstruction with each method (Section 2.2.1), re-evaluating localization error and spatial correlation with the ground truth as before.

Localization error increased for every method as SNR decreased (@fig-noise-localization), but wMNE alone accounts for most of that pattern: already several times wCSET's error at the highest SNR tested (median `{python} noise_loc_wmne_median20` mm at SNR=20), it climbed steadily worse from there and was significantly worse than wCSET across the entire SNR range tested (region-paired cluster-permutation, p_corrected `{python} noise_loc_wmne_p`, Cohen's dz = `{python} noise_loc_wmne_dz`), reaching `{python} noise_loc_wmne_median1` mm by SNR=1. The other four methods (wCSET, CSET, sLORETA, dSPM) instead behaved similarly to one another, staying low until roughly SNR=3–5 before climbing. sLORETA's and dSPM's high-SNR plateaus did reach significance against wCSET (SNR=`{python} noise_loc_sloreta_snr`–`{python} noise_loc_sloreta_snr_end`, p_corrected `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_p`; SNR=`{python} noise_loc_dspm_snr_start`–`{python} noise_loc_dspm_snr_end`, p_corrected `{python} noise_loc_dspm_p`), but with modest effect sizes (dz = `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_dz` and `{python} noise_loc_dspm_dz` respectively) that didn't extend to lower SNR; CSET's own curve never diverged from wCSET's enough to register even a candidate cluster anywhere in the range tested — a stronger statement than "not significant," since no cluster (and so no p-value or effect size) exists to report.

```{python filename="simf_localization_noise_plot.py"}

Markers are filled/solid where wCSET's error is significantly lower than the competitor's (region-paired cluster-permutation); wCSET is the reference."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

noise_loc_fig, noise_loc_ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
noise_loc_fig, noise_loc_ax = noise_metrics.plot.cluster_permutation(
    noise_loc_results, colors=COLORS, marker="o", markersize=5, ax=noise_loc_ax,

noise_loc_ax.set_xscale("log")

noise_loc_ax.set_ylabel("Localization error (mm)")

plt.tight_layout()
```

For spatial correlation with the ground truth (@fig-noise-correlation), wCSET significantly outperformed all four competitors at both the quarter rising phase and the peak, down to SNR=`{python} noise_corr_end_std` (SNR=`{python} noise_corr_end_cset` against CSET; region-paired cluster-permutation, all p_corrected `{python} noise_corr_p_all`; effect sizes ranging from dz = `{python} noise_corr_dz_min` vs. `{python} noise_corr_dz_min_label` to dz = `{python} noise_corr_dz_max` vs. `{python} noise_corr_dz_max_label`) , even as correlation declined monotonically for every method (e.g. wCSET: `{python} noise_corr_wcset_qrp20`→`{python} noise_corr_wcset_qrp1` at quarter rising phase and `{python} noise_corr_wcset_pp20`→`{python} noise_corr_wcset_pp1` at peak, from SNR=20 to SNR=1). Below that, correlations for every method had collapsed toward zero, and wCSET's was slightly but significantly lower (all p_corrected ≤ `{python} noise_corr_worse_p_max`).

### Robustness to Prior Noise — Full Results (Section 3.1.3)

```{python filename="simf_degradation_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# per explicit instruction, only the permutation experiment is shown here
# (deletion/addition still computed and saved by processing_simf.qmd's
# Statistics section, just not plotted or discussed in this document).
operator = "permutation"

deg_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("../results/simf/degradation")

# --- localization error --- reference=sLORETA (doesn't degrade),
# competitors=CSET/wCSET: tests when a corrupted connectome makes CSET/
# wCSET perform significantly worse than using no connectome at all,
# rather than a relative CSET-vs-wCSET comparison. Identical call to the
# one already cached by processing_simf.qmd's Statistics section.
# phase="qrp" always (no pp counterpart exists for this metric).
deg_comparisons = deg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["sloreta"], ["cset", "wcset"])
pct_order = sorted(deg_metrics.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp"})["percentage"].unique())
loc_result = deg_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation(
    "localization_error", coord="percentage", group_by="Method", comparisons=deg_comparisons,
    pairing_col="region", coord_order=pct_order, higher_is_better=False, filters={"phase": "qrp"},
    n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
)
loc_clusters_cset = loc_result.clusters_by_pair[("sloreta", "cset")]
loc_clusters_wcset = loc_result.clusters_by_pair[("sloreta", "wcset")]

# --- spatial correlation --- same sLORETA-reference comparison as
# above. phase="qrp" always (no pp counterpart is computed for
# degradation, see degradation_reconstruction.py).
pct_order_c = sorted(deg_metrics.to_df(metrics="correlation", filters={"phase": "qrp"})["percentage"].unique())
corr_result = deg_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation(
    "correlation", coord="percentage", group_by="Method", comparisons=deg_comparisons,
    pairing_col="region", coord_order=pct_order_c, higher_is_better=True, filters={"phase": "qrp"},
    n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
)
corr_clusters_cset = corr_result.clusters_by_pair[("sloreta", "cset")]
corr_clusters_wcset = corr_result.clusters_by_pair[("sloreta", "wcset")]

# --- statistics quoted in the prose below --- dz is negated so that positive = CSET/wCSET better
# (the main text's convention). Clusters are selected by sign rather
# than by cluster position/count: how many clusters exist (and where)
# depends on the current simulation parameters (see
# parameter_estimates_review.md) and isn't safe to hard-code - a prior
# version of this cell assumed fixed counts per pair and broke (IndexError)
# once results/simf/degradation was regenerated under retuned physical
# parameters. Per cluster_permutation_mne's sign convention, sign=-1 means
# the competitor (CSET/wCSET) significantly beats sLORETA, sign=+1 means
# sLORETA significantly beats the competitor; `cluster_where` returns None
# when no cluster of that sign exists (currently the case for loc/wcset's
# "worse" cluster - see prose, wCSET no longer becomes significantly worse
# than sLORETA on localization error at any tested degradation level).
# main_cluster()'s own significance caveat applies to each cluster
# individually here too - corr/wcset's "worse" cluster does NOT survive FDR
# correction (p_corrected `0.069` > 0.05), so the prose below must describe
# it as a trend, not a significant effect.

def cluster_where(cluster_df, sign):
    """The cluster (if any) where the competitor significantly beats
    sLORETA (sign=-1) or sLORETA significantly beats the competitor
    (sign=1) - None if no such cluster exists in the current result."""
    rows = cluster_df[cluster_df["sign"] == sign]
    return rows.iloc[0] if not rows.empty else None

deg_loc_cset_better = cluster_where(loc_clusters_cset, -1)
deg_loc_cset_better_end = fmt_num(deg_loc_cset_better["percentage_end"], 0)
deg_loc_cset_better_p, deg_loc_cset_better_dz = fmt_p(deg_loc_cset_better["p_corrected"]), fmt_stat(-deg_loc_cset_better["effect_size"])

deg_loc_cset_c = cluster_where(loc_clusters_cset, 1)
deg_loc_cset_p, deg_loc_cset_dz = fmt_p(deg_loc_cset_c["p_corrected"]), fmt_stat(-deg_loc_cset_c["effect_size"])
deg_loc_cset_start = fmt_num(deg_loc_cset_c["percentage_start"], 0)

deg_loc_wcset_early = cluster_where(loc_clusters_wcset, -1)
deg_loc_wcset_early_end = fmt_num(deg_loc_wcset_early["percentage_end"], 0)
deg_loc_wcset_early_p, deg_loc_wcset_early_dz = fmt_p(deg_loc_wcset_early["p_corrected"]), fmt_stat(-deg_loc_wcset_early["effect_size"])
deg_loc_wcset_worse = cluster_where(loc_clusters_wcset, 1)  # None under current results - see prose

deg_corr_cset_early = cluster_where(corr_clusters_cset, -1)
deg_corr_cset_early_p, deg_corr_cset_early_dz = fmt_p(deg_corr_cset_early["p_corrected"]), fmt_stat(-deg_corr_cset_early["effect_size"])
deg_corr_cset_early_end = fmt_num(deg_corr_cset_early["percentage_end"], 0)
deg_corr_cset_late = cluster_where(corr_clusters_cset, 1)
deg_corr_cset_late_p, deg_corr_cset_late_dz = fmt_p(deg_corr_cset_late["p_corrected"]), fmt_stat(-deg_corr_cset_late["effect_size"])
deg_corr_cset_late_start = fmt_num(deg_corr_cset_late["percentage_start"], 0)

deg_corr_wcset_early = cluster_where(corr_clusters_wcset, -1)
deg_corr_wcset_early_p, deg_corr_wcset_early_dz = fmt_p(deg_corr_wcset_early["p_corrected"]), fmt_stat(-deg_corr_wcset_early["effect_size"])
deg_corr_wcset_early_end = fmt_num(deg_corr_wcset_early["percentage_end"], 0)
deg_corr_wcset_late = cluster_where(corr_clusters_wcset, 1)
deg_corr_wcset_late_p = fmt_p(deg_corr_wcset_late["p_corrected"])  # does not survive correction - quoted as a trend only

# localization/correlation medians quoted in prose - read from
# processing_simf.qmd's precomputed metadata["derived"], not recomputed here.
_perm_d = deg_metrics.metadata["derived"]
deg_loc_perm_wcset_lo, deg_loc_perm_wcset_hi = _perm_d["loc_wcset_0_60"]
deg_loc_perm_wcset_70 = _perm_d["loc_wcset_70"]
deg_loc_perm_wcset_100 = _perm_d["loc_wcset_100"]

deg_loc_perm_wcset_lo_s = fmt_num(deg_loc_perm_wcset_lo)
deg_loc_perm_wcset_hi_s = fmt_num(deg_loc_perm_wcset_hi)
deg_loc_perm_wcset_70_s = fmt_num(deg_loc_perm_wcset_70)
deg_loc_perm_wcset_100_s = fmt_num(deg_loc_perm_wcset_100)

deg_corr_perm_wcset_0 = fmt_num(_perm_d["corr_wcset_0"], 2)
deg_corr_perm_wcset_100 = fmt_num(_perm_d["corr_wcset_100"], 2)
_cset_lo, _cset_hi = _perm_d["corr_cset_0_60"]
deg_corr_perm_cset_lo = fmt_num(_cset_lo, 2)
deg_corr_perm_cset_hi = fmt_num(_cset_hi, 2)
deg_corr_perm_cset_100 = fmt_num(_perm_d["corr_cset_100"], 2)
```

Using the connectome-perturbation procedure of Section 2.2.1, we re-evaluated localization error (@fig-degradation-localization) and spatial correlation (@fig-degradation-correlation) for CSET and wCSET, benchmarked directly against sLORETA rather than against each other: sLORETA is connectome-agnostic, so its performance cannot be affected by connectome corruption, making it a natural floor — the degradation level at which a connectivity-informed method becomes significantly worse than sLORETA is the point past which using the (corrupted) connectome is actively counterproductive, rather than merely less helpful. dSPM remains connectome-agnostic too and is shown only as a flat, untested reference line.

wCSET's localization error remained essentially flat under permutation up to 60% (`{python} deg_loc_perm_wcset_lo_s`–`{python} deg_loc_perm_wcset_hi_s` mm), only climbing noticeably beyond that point (`{python} deg_loc_perm_wcset_70_s` mm at 70%, `{python} deg_loc_perm_wcset_100_s` mm at 100%). Benchmarked against sLORETA (region-paired cluster-permutation; positive dz = CSET/wCSET better), wCSET was significantly *more* accurate across low-to-moderate degradation (0–`{python} deg_loc_wcset_early_end`%, p_corrected `{python} deg_loc_wcset_early_p`, Cohen's dz = `{python} deg_loc_wcset_early_dz`), and never became significantly worse than sLORETA at any degradation level tested, including full (100%) permutation. CSET showed the same early advantage over a comparable range (0–`{python} deg_loc_cset_better_end`%, p_corrected `{python} deg_loc_cset_better_p`, dz = `{python} deg_loc_cset_better_dz`), but unlike wCSET this advantage reversed: CSET became significantly worse than sLORETA from `{python} deg_loc_cset_start`% onward (p_corrected `{python} deg_loc_cset_p`, dz = `{python} deg_loc_cset_dz`) — a degradation level at which wCSET's own localization error never reached a significant deficit, even under full connectome permutation.

```{python filename="simf_localization_degradation_plot.py"}

Markers are filled/solid where significantly different from sLORETA, tested at each degradation level (region-paired cluster-permutation). Dashed line: dSPM's undegraded-connectome reference level."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

# flat reference: dSPM is connectome-agnostic (not recomputed per
# degradation level), so its flagship (undegraded) median is reused as-is

# prose above).
deg_ref_loc = deg_metrics.metadata["derived"]["ref_loc"]

# two-pair result (sLORETA vs CSET, sLORETA vs wCSET) -> plot.cluster_permutation()
# dispatches to the compact multi-competitor overlay (same pattern as the
# noise-sweep figures above, simf_noise_stats.py), reference (sLORETA)
# auto-inferred from the group shared by both pairs.
deg_loc_fig, deg_loc_ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
deg_loc_fig, deg_loc_ax = deg_metrics.plot.cluster_permutation(
    loc_result, colors=COLORS, marker="o", markersize=4, ax=deg_loc_ax,
)
mark_reference(deg_loc_ax, "sloreta")
# dSPM stays a flat, untested reference line (still connectome-agnostic,
# just not part of this comparison) - sLORETA no longer needs one, it's
# plotted as its own tested curve above.
deg_loc_ax.axhline(deg_ref_loc["dspm"], color=COLORS["dspm"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5, zorder=0.5)
deg_loc_ax.set_xlabel("Connectome degradation (%)")
deg_loc_ax.set_ylabel("Localization error (mm)")
deg_loc_ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

legend_handles = [
    Line2D([0], [0], color=COLORS["dspm"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5, label="dspm (undegraded)"),
]
deg_loc_fig.legend(handles=legend_handles, loc="lower center", ncol=1, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.04))

deg_loc_fig.tight_layout()
```


Spatial correlation with the ground truth showed a similar but more pronounced pattern: permutation slowly degraded wCSET's correlation (`{python} deg_corr_perm_wcset_0` at 0% down to `{python} deg_corr_perm_wcset_100` at 100%), while CSET's own correlation stayed comparatively flat through 60% (`{python} deg_corr_perm_cset_lo`–`{python} deg_corr_perm_cset_hi`) before also declining sharply thereafter (`{python} deg_corr_perm_cset_100` at 100%). Against sLORETA, both methods started out significantly better (region-paired cluster-permutation: CSET 0–`{python} deg_corr_cset_early_end`%, p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_cset_early_p`, dz = `{python} deg_corr_cset_early_dz`; wCSET 0–`{python} deg_corr_wcset_early_end`%, p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_wcset_early_p`, dz = `{python} deg_corr_wcset_early_dz`), but only CSET's advantage reversed into a significant deficit, from `{python} deg_corr_cset_late_start`% onward (p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_cset_late_p`, dz = `{python} deg_corr_cset_late_dz`). wCSET's correlation, by contrast, never became significantly worse than sLORETA's, even at full permutation — its apparent dip at 100% did not reach significance (p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_wcset_late_p`).

### Surrogate alternatives — Full Results (Section 3.1.4)

```{python filename="simf_surrogate_full_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# self-contained, like the other "Full Results" Annex sections above -
# reloads and recomputes independently of the main-text surrogate cell
# rather than reusing its variables (same identical calls, disk-cache hit).
surrogates_full = ["beltrami", "fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin"]
conditions_full = ["original"] + surrogates_full

# same reader-facing renaming as the main-text cell (Section 3.1.4) - fused/
# fused-bin/geom-atlas/geom-atlas-bin are the on-disk `Surrogate` tags.
SURROGATE_LABELS_FULL = {
    "fused": "atlas", "fused-bin": "atlas-bin",
    "geom-atlas": "local", "geom-atlas-bin": "local-bin",
}

surr_metrics_full = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("../results/simf/surrogates")
surr_comparisons_full = surr_metrics_full.stat.build_comparisons(["original"], surrogates_full)

# CSET's own breakdown - wCSET's is reported in full in the main text.
surr_loc_cset = surr_metrics_full.stat.wilcoxon(
    "localization_error", group_by="Surrogate",
    comparisons=surr_comparisons_full, pairing_col="region",
    filters={"Method": "cset", "phase": "qrp"},
)
surr_corr_cset = {}
for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]:
    surr_corr_cset[phase] = surr_metrics_full.stat.wilcoxon(
        "correlation", group_by="Surrogate",
        comparisons=surr_comparisons_full, pairing_col="region",
        filters={"Method": "cset", "phase": phase},
    )

# statistics quoted in the prose below (effects as stored: original - surrogate).
_loc_cset = surr_loc_cset.vs("original")
_corr_cset = {ph: surr_corr_cset[ph].vs("original") for ph in ["qrp", "pp"]}
loc_cset_p = {s: fmt_p(_loc_cset.loc[s, "p_corrected"]) for s in surrogates_full}
loc_cset_r = {s: fmt_stat(_loc_cset.loc[s, "effect"]) for s in surrogates_full}
corr_cset_p = {(s, ph): fmt_p(_corr_cset[ph].loc[s, "p_corrected"]) for ph in _corr_cset for s in surrogates_full}
corr_cset_r = {(s, ph): fmt_stat(_corr_cset[ph].loc[s, "effect"]) for ph in _corr_cset for s in surrogates_full}
```

This section reports CSET's full surrogate-connectome breakdown (@fig-surrogate-cset), summarized qualitatively in the main text alongside wCSET's own (Section 3.1.4), which is reported there in full.

For localization error, CSET was significantly less accurate with beltrami (p_corrected `{python} loc_cset_p['beltrami']`, r = `{python} loc_cset_r['beltrami']`) and the local surrogate (p_corrected `{python} loc_cset_p['geom-atlas']`, r = `{python} loc_cset_r['geom-atlas']`); the atlas, atlas-bin, and local-bin surrogates did not differ significantly from the original connectome (p_corrected `{python} loc_cset_p['fused']`, `{python} loc_cset_p['fused-bin']`, and `{python} loc_cset_p['geom-atlas-bin']` respectively).

For spatial correlation, CSET was significantly lower than the original connectome with the atlas surrogate at both the quarter rising phase (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('fused', 'qrp')]`) and the peak (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('fused', 'pp')]`), and likewise with the local (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('geom-atlas', 'qrp')]` and `{python} corr_cset_p[('geom-atlas', 'pp')]`) and local-bin (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('geom-atlas-bin', 'qrp')]` and `{python} corr_cset_p[('geom-atlas-bin', 'pp')]`) surrogates at both phases. The atlas-bin surrogate reached significance only at the peak (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('fused-bin', 'pp')]`), not at the quarter rising phase (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('fused-bin', 'qrp')]`). Beltrami never differed significantly from the original connectome, at either phase (p_corrected `{python} corr_cset_p[('beltrami', 'qrp')]` and `{python} corr_cset_p[('beltrami', 'pp')]`).

```{python filename="simf_surrogate_cset_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-surrogate-cset
#| fig-cap: "CSET accuracy using the true structural connectome versus five dMRI-free connectome surrogates (subject sub-10; box = IQR, line = median). (a) Localization error (mm) at the quarter rising phase. (b, c) Spatial correlation with ground truth at the quarter rising phase (b) and peak phase (c). Dashed lines mark dSPM's and sLORETA's true-connectome medians as reference. Stars mark significance vs. the original (true) connectome (Wilcoxon signed-rank, region-paired, FDR-corrected). wCSET's equivalent comparisons are reported in Figure 4 of the main text."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

CONDITION_COLORS_FULL = {
    "original": LINE_COLOR,
    "beltrami": "#2a78d6",
    "fused": "#eb6834",
    "fused-bin": "#1baf7a",
    "geom-atlas": "#eda100",
    "geom-atlas-bin": "#e87ba4",
}

surr_ref_loc_full = surr_metrics_full.metadata["derived"]["ref_loc"]
surr_ref_corr_full = surr_metrics_full.metadata["derived"]["ref_corr"]
ref_methods_full = ["dspm", "sloreta"]
phase_titles_full = {"qrp": "Quarter rising phase", "pp": "Peak phase"}
panel_letters_full = {"loc": "a", "qrp": "b", "pp": "c"}

def surr_cset_panel(result, ax, ref_medians):
    """Boxes per connectome condition, stars vs. the original, dSPM/sLORETA medians as dashed lines."""
    surr_metrics_full.plot.group_comparison(
        result, order=conditions_full, palette=CONDITION_COLORS_FULL, points=False, showfliers=False, width=0.6,
        tick_labels=SURROGATE_LABELS_FULL, reference_suffix=" (ref.)", ax=ax,
        reference_lines={f"{METHOD_LABELS[m]} (original connectome)": (ref_medians[m], COLORS[m]) for m in ref_methods_full},
    )
    plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right")
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

surr_cset_fig, surr_cset_axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(len(conditions_full) * 1.3 * 2.4, 5.5))

# panel a: localization error at qrp.
ax_loc_cset = surr_cset_axes[0]
surr_cset_panel(surr_loc_cset, ax_loc_cset, surr_ref_loc_full)
ax_loc_cset.set_ylabel("Localization error (mm)")
ax_loc_cset.set_title(f"{panel_letters_full['loc']}. Localization error\n(quarter rising phase)")

# panels b, c: spatial correlation at qrp / peak phase, sharing a y-scale.
corr_axes_cset = {}
for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]:
    ax = surr_cset_axes[1 if phase == "qrp" else 2]
    corr_axes_cset[phase] = ax
    surr_cset_panel(surr_corr_cset[phase], ax, surr_ref_corr_full[phase])
    ax.set_ylabel("Spatial correlation")
    ax.set_title(f"{panel_letters_full[phase]}. {phase_titles_full[phase]}")
for ax in corr_axes_cset.values():
    ax.set_ylim(0, 0.9)

surr_cset_fig.legend(*ax_loc_cset.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="lower center", ncol=2, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.04))

plt.tight_layout()
```

## Study III: Clinical Dynamics (Simultaneous iEEG/EEG)

### Spatial Correlation Analysis — Full Results, All Subjects (Section 3.3.1)

This section reports both polarity-invariant spatial metrics of Study III (amplitude rank correlation and AUC on |amplitude|; Sections 2.3.2 and 2.3.3) for all four Clinical Dataset B subjects, with the per-method AUC that the main text leaves out (@fig-intracranial-diff of the main text shows Subjects 1 and 2, sub-48 and sub-34). Sub-12 and sub-50 had deep sources, far from the cortical source space (Section 2.2.3): their EEG-derived reconstruction, and the virtual iEEG projected from it, is inherently less reliable, so their results are reported here rather than pooled into the main comparison. Statistics are the same autocorrelation-corrected paired tests as in the main text (Section 2.4.2).

```{python filename="intra_spatial_full_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import mindmap as mm

# Self-contained, like the other Annex sections above: reloads the suite written by
# processing_intra.qmd ("Spatial pattern metrics") and repeats index.qmd's own
# stat.ttest_ess() calls (disk-cache hit).
SPATIAL_DIR = "../results/intra/spatial_metrics"
full_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load(SPATIAL_DIR)
full_null = pd.read_csv(f"{SPATIAL_DIR}/null.csv", dtype={"Subject": str})
COMPETITORS = ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]
FULL_ORDER = ["wcset"] + COMPETITORS
FULL_SUBJECTS = ["48", "34", "12", "50"]
FULL_TITLES = {"48": "Subject 1 (sub-48)", "34": "Subject 2 (sub-34)",
               "12": "sub-12 (deep source)", "50": "sub-50 (deep source)"}
FULL_METRICS = {"correlation_spatial_absrank": ("amplitude rank correlation", 0.0), "auc_spatial": ("AUC on |amplitude|", 0.5)}

full_wide, full_results = {}, {}
for metric in FULL_METRICS:
    for subject in FULL_SUBJECTS:
        wide = (full_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"Subject": subject})
                .pivot_table(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").dropna())
        full_wide[(subject, metric)] = wide
        full_results[(subject, metric)] = full_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
            metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=full_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
            pairing_col="times", subject_order=wide.index.tolist(), filters={"Subject": subject},
        )

# one row per competitor: p-values and Cohen's dz (positive = wCSET better)
full_vs = {k: r.vs("wcset") for k, r in full_results.items()}

def full_effect(subject, metric, competitor):
    return full_vs[(subject, metric)].loc[competitor, "effect"]

def full_p(subject, metric, competitor):
    return full_vs[(subject, metric)].loc[competitor, "p_corrected"]

# statistics quoted in the prose below: every significant comparison for the two deep-source subjects
_sig = [(s, m, c) for s in ["12", "50"] for m in FULL_METRICS for c in COMPETITORS if full_p(s, m, c) < 0.05]
full_deep_sig = "; ".join(
    f"sub-{s_}, {FULL_METRICS[m][0]}, wCSET vs. {METHOD_LABELS[c]}: p_corrected {fmt_p(full_p(s_, m, c))}, dz = {fmt_stat(full_effect(s_, m, c))}"
    for s_, m, c in _sig
) or "none"
full_deep_n_sig = len(_sig)
full_50_p_min = fmt_p(min(full_p("50", m, c) for m in FULL_METRICS for c in COMPETITORS))
full_12_auc_wcset = fmt_num(full_wide[("12", "auc_spatial")]["wcset"].median(), 2)
full_12_auc_std_lo = fmt_num(min(full_wide[("12", "auc_spatial")][c].median() for c in ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne"]), 2)
full_12_auc_std_hi = fmt_num(max(full_wide[("12", "auc_spatial")][c].median() for c in ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne"]), 2)
```

For sub-12, wCSET had the highest median AUC of all methods (median `{python} full_12_auc_wcset`, sLORETA, CSET, dSPM, and wMNE `{python} full_12_auc_std_lo`–`{python} full_12_auc_std_hi`; @fig-intra-full), but only its advantage over CSET reached significance. For sub-50, every method stayed close to zero rank correlation and 0.5 AUC, and no comparison was significant (smallest p_corrected `{python} full_50_p_min`). Across both deep-source subjects, `{python} full_deep_n_sig` comparison(s) reached significance (`{python} full_deep_sig`), all in wCSET's favor, and wCSET was never significantly worse than any other method. This matches the Discussion's framing: for these subjects, no method's reconstruction tracked the recording well enough to clearly distinguish one from another.

```{python filename="intra_spatial_full_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-intra-full
#| fig-cap: "Spatial agreement between virtual and recorded iEEG for all four Clinical Dataset B subjects (columns); Subjects 1 and 2 are the main-text subjects, sub-12 and sub-50 had deep sources, far from the cortical source space. Rows 1–2: amplitude rank correlation (Spearman ρ across contacts between recorded and virtual absolute amplitude); rows 3–4: AUC on |amplitude| (spatial overlap, active contacts = at least 30% of the recorded maximum). Both ignore the sign of the contacts; the signed correlation is shown in @fig-intra-signed. Rows 1 and 3: value per method at each timepoint of the comparison window (box = IQR, line = median, outliers hidden); dotted line = chance value (ρ = 0, AUC = 0.5). Rows 2 and 4: paired difference, wCSET minus each other method, one value per timepoint (violin = distribution, thick line = median, thin line = IQR); positive = wCSET better. Above each violin: significance from a paired t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (FDR-corrected; *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001), Cohen's dz (positive = wCSET better), and the percentage of timepoints at which wCSET's value exceeds the other method's, relative to 50%."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

full_fig, full_axes = plt.subplots(2 * len(FULL_METRICS), len(FULL_SUBJECTS), figsize=(4.4 * len(FULL_SUBJECTS), 16),
                                   gridspec_kw={"hspace": 0.55, "wspace": 0.3}, squeeze=False)
for m_i, (metric, (label, chance)) in enumerate(FULL_METRICS.items()):
    for col, subject in enumerate(FULL_SUBJECTS):
        result = full_results[(subject, metric)]

        # value per method
        ax = full_axes[2 * m_i, col]
        full_metrics.plot.group_comparison(
            result, order=FULL_ORDER, palette=COLORS, points=False, showfliers=False, width=0.55, alpha=0,
            saturation=1, fill_alpha=FILL_ALPHA, chance_value=chance, tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, reference_suffix=" (ref.)", ax=ax,
        )
        plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
        ax.set_xlabel("")
        ax.set_ylabel(label if col == 0 else "", fontsize=8)
        ax.set_title(f"{FULL_TITLES[subject]}:\n{label} per method", loc="left", fontsize=9)
        ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

        # paired differences, positive = wCSET better
        dax = full_axes[2 * m_i + 1, col]
        full_metrics.plot.paired_differences(
            result, reference="wcset", order=COMPETITORS, palette=COLORS,
            annotate=("stars", "effect", "winrate"), tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, ax=dax,
        )
        plt.setp(dax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
        dax.set_title(f"{FULL_TITLES[subject]}:\n{label}, wCSET − method", loc="left", fontsize=9)
        if col == 0:
            dax.set_ylabel(f"wCSET − method\n({label})", fontsize=8)
    share_ylim(full_axes[2 * m_i])  # per-method row comparable across subjects
plt.show()
```

**Signed spatial correlation.** The main text compares virtual and recorded iEEG with sign-free measures only, because the polarity of intracranial contacts is not interpreted. @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026 report the signed (Pearson) spatial correlation across contacts instead; @fig-intra-signed shows that measure for all four subjects, with the same paired tests and the permutation chance range of Section 2.4.1, for direct comparison with their work.

```{python filename="intra_signed_full_stats.py"}
#| output: false
# Signed Pearson correlation across contacts, computed by processing_intra.qmd alongside the
# sign-free metrics; same per-subject paired tests as above.
SIGNED = "correlation_spatial_signed"
STANDARD = ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne"]

signed_wide, signed_results = {}, {}
for subject in FULL_SUBJECTS:
    wide = (full_metrics.to_df(metrics=SIGNED, filters={"Subject": subject})
            .pivot_table(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").dropna())
    signed_wide[subject] = wide
    signed_results[subject] = full_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
        SIGNED, group_by="Method", comparisons=full_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
        pairing_col="times", subject_order=wide.index.tolist(), filters={"Subject": subject},
    )
signed_vs = {s_: r.vs("wcset") for s_, r in signed_results.items()}

def signed_chance(subject):
    d = full_null[(full_null["Metric"] == SIGNED) & (full_null["Subject"] == subject)]
    return d["null_lo"].mean(), d["null_hi"].mean()

# statistics quoted in the prose (Subject 1 = sub-48; positive dz = wCSET better)
signed_48_wcset = fmt_num(signed_wide["48"]["wcset"].median(), 2)
signed_48_std_lo = fmt_num(min(signed_wide["48"][c].median() for c in STANDARD), 2)
signed_48_std_hi = fmt_num(max(signed_wide["48"][c].median() for c in STANDARD), 2)
signed_48_chance = fmt_num(signed_chance("48")[1], 2)
signed_48_p_max = fmt_p(signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
signed_48_dz_lo = fmt_stat(signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
signed_48_dz_hi = fmt_stat(signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
signed_48_p_beltrami = fmt_p(signed_vs["48"].loc["beltrami", "p_corrected"])
signed_others_p_min = fmt_p(min(signed_vs[s_]["p_corrected"].min() for s_ in ["34", "12", "50"]))
```

In Subject 1, wCSET's virtual iEEG correlated with the recording above the chance range (median r = `{python} signed_48_wcset`, chance range up to `{python} signed_48_chance`), whereas sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET did not (medians `{python} signed_48_std_lo` to `{python} signed_48_std_hi`). wCSET's correlation was significantly higher than these four methods' (largest p_corrected `{python} signed_48_p_max`, dz = `{python} signed_48_dz_lo`–`{python} signed_48_dz_hi`), and did not differ from Beltrami's (p_corrected `{python} signed_48_p_beltrami`). No comparison was significant in the other three subjects (smallest p_corrected `{python} signed_others_p_min`). These are the same conclusions as with the sign-free measures of the main text, with larger effects in Subject 1.

```{python filename="intra_signed_full_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-intra-signed
#| fig-cap: "Signed spatial correlation (Pearson r across contacts, as reported by Grova et al. 2016 and Afnan et al. 2026) between virtual and recorded iEEG, for all four Clinical Dataset B subjects (columns). Row 1: value per method at each timepoint of the comparison window (box = IQR, line = median, outliers hidden); gray band = chance range, the 2.5–97.5th percentiles after randomly permuting contact labels (1000 permutations, averaged over timepoints and methods); dotted line = 0. Row 2: paired difference, wCSET minus each other method, one value per timepoint (violin = distribution, thick line = median, thin line = IQR); positive = wCSET better. Above each violin: significance from a paired t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (FDR-corrected; *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001), Cohen's dz (positive = wCSET better), and the percentage of timepoints at which wCSET's value exceeds the other method's, relative to 50%."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

signed_fig, signed_axes = plt.subplots(2, len(FULL_SUBJECTS), figsize=(4.4 * len(FULL_SUBJECTS), 8),
                                       gridspec_kw={"hspace": 0.55, "wspace": 0.3}, squeeze=False)
for col, subject in enumerate(FULL_SUBJECTS):
    ax = signed_axes[0, col]
    full_metrics.plot.group_comparison(
        signed_results[subject], order=FULL_ORDER, palette=COLORS, points=False, showfliers=False, width=0.55,
        alpha=0, saturation=1, fill_alpha=FILL_ALPHA, chance=signed_chance(subject), chance_value=0,
        tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, reference_suffix=" (ref.)", ax=ax,
    )
    plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.set_ylabel("Signed spatial correlation (r)" if col == 0 else "", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(f"{FULL_TITLES[subject]}:\nsigned spatial correlation per method", loc="left", fontsize=9)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

    dax = signed_axes[1, col]
    full_metrics.plot.paired_differences(
        signed_results[subject], reference="wcset", order=COMPETITORS, palette=COLORS,
        annotate=("stars", "effect", "winrate"), tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, ax=dax,
    )
    plt.setp(dax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
    dax.set_title(f"{FULL_TITLES[subject]}:\nsigned spatial correlation, wCSET − method", loc="left", fontsize=9)
    if col == 0:
        dax.set_ylabel("wCSET − method\n(signed spatial correlation)", fontsize=8)
share_ylim(signed_axes[0])
plt.show()
```
